subject: Portfolio assistant fallback
text:
When Gemini fails, the chat assistant on my portfolio still answers, with no AI model at all. It got 92.5% of test questions right.

Without a backup, a failed Gemini call means a recruiter's question gets no answer. So I built one that runs in the browser: every fact on the site (each job, project, skill and certificate) is stored as a short passage, a question is matched to passages by keywords and by meaning, and a small ranking model picks the best one. The answer is that passage with its source, so it can't make anything up.

To test it, I wrote 120 questions a recruiter might ask, including typos and questions it should refuse, like salary, visa status and skills not in my profile. I tuned on 80 and kept 40 aside until the end. The 92.5% is on those 40.

The biggest gain came from teaching it when not to answer. Refusing when the ranking model's confidence is low added 4 points, and fixed refusal topics for pay, work authorization and personal details added 7. Together that is more than the ranking model itself added, 10 points.

Speed was the other problem: the first version took 7.5 s per answer. Shorter inputs and a smaller ranking model brought it to 0.9 s, and its 57 MB of files download only the first time Gemini fails. It still misses some vague questions, like "what has he been working on recently".

So a recruiter who asks about my work gets an answer quoted from my own profile, with its source, even when the AI behind the site is down.

If you've built retrieval over a small set of documents, how do you decide when it should refuse instead of answer?

#MachineLearning #NLP
alt_text: Scatter chart of test questions answered right against download size for each assistant design: keywords only 63 percent at 0 MB, with decline rules 70 percent, MiniLM with the L6 reranker 83 percent at 46 MB, MiniLM with L12 85 percent and 90 percent with decline rules at 57 MB, bge-small with L12 92.5 percent at 68 MB. The shipped design, bge-small with L6, reaches 92.5 percent at 57 MB and about 0.9 seconds per answer.

subject: Tax Anomaly Audit Compliance Engine
text:
An auditor checking a ledger in order opens 1,108 entries to find 90% of the problems. Sorted by my risk score, they open 43.

The ledger is simulated. I generated the entries and planted 47 problems, listed in a separate table that the detection code never reads, so every result can be checked against the right answers.

Each entry gets three checks. Benford's Law: in many real financial datasets about 30% of amounts start with 1, so amounts that break that pattern score higher. An Isolation Forest, a model that flags amounts and tax ratios unlike the rest. And a tax-rate rule that flags any claim whose rate doesn't match its category. The pipeline runs in Dagster, so each step can be rerun on its own.

Scoring each check on its own changed how I read the results. The plain tax-rate rule found 45 of the 47 problems and flagged nothing wrongly. The model found 18, and the rule had already found all 18.

So the rule's 45 flags go first, and every one is a real problem: that alone gets an auditor to 90% in 43 entries. The model and Benford's Law rank the rest, and the 2 problems the rule missed come up at entries 131 and 137 of 1,200.

On a real ledger I would start the same way: measure the simple rules alone first, then use a model to rank what they leave.

How do you get labels for a real ledger when nobody plants the answers?

#DataEngineering #AnomalyDetection
alt_text: Line chart of planted anomalies found against entries opened, on simulated data. In risk order, 90 percent of anomalies are found after 43 entries; in ledger order it takes 1,108. 96 percent less review work for the same 90 percent.

subject: Member Messages QA System: Semantic Search & NER-Based Question Answering
text:
I chose embeddings-based semantic search for member questions, ruling out fine-tuned LLMs, knowledge graphs, and rule-based matching.

To answer natural-language questions about member data, I built an interactive /ask API that ranks unstructured messages by cosine similarity over SentenceTransformer embeddings, combined with spaCy named entity recognition and fuzzy first-name matching.

Retrieving unstructured text can easily pull a message that matches the subject but contains the wrong event details, so the system needed to prove how accurate it was at finding the correct member, message, and answer for a given question.

So I ran eval_qa.py to score 26 hand-written, paraphrased questions against a labelled evaluation set.

The answer was that member identification accuracy reached 100%, while message retrieval accuracy and answer extraction accuracy both reached 96%. The one miss asks for Lorenzo's Thursday booking, where the top-ranked message is his Saturday dinner at The Fat Duck. That result led to a clear threshold: CI fails if answer accuracy drops below 90%.

This system now answers natural-language questions about members directly from unstructured message text.

When your semantic search retriever pulls a message for the wrong day of the week, do you fix that in pre-filtering or during answer extraction?

subject: Multi-State Land Use Emissions Analysis
text:
Forecasting emissions by copying last year beats two standard models on real state data.

When forests burn or farmland turns into suburbs, a state stores or releases a different amount of carbon. I wanted to learn how that is measured from public records, so Multi-State Land Use Emissions Analysis processes daily land-cover data for five U.S. states. The daily files are simulated, but the emission factors and historical inventory come from the EPA.

Change like this is often slow, so predicting next year as a copy of this one is a strong competitor. To see if learning from history helps more than repetition, I compared Linear Regression and Random Forest against that naive baseline.

The test used the EPA's 25 annual series. I trained on data up to 2017 and scored predictions for 2018 through 2022. Linear Regression reached an accuracy of 0.9418 and Random Forest 0.9329. Copying the previous value reached 0.947.

Neither one beat it, so the report now shows the copy-last-year number next to every score.

If you forecast a slow-moving series, do you report a copy-last-year baseline next to every model score?

#DataEngineering #MachineLearning

subject: Job Market Lakehouse
text:
A June 2025 query on my job market lakehouse read 3,015 of its 60,000 rows. Hive never opened the other 19 months.

I built the lakehouse to learn how a whole data system fits together, from raw files to checked output. With AI changing how work gets done, I think an engineer has to stay broad and keep adapting.

The pipeline runs on simulated job postings from 400 companies. PySpark transforms them, 11 Great Expectations checks gate the output, Airflow runs the steps, and a HiveQL table keeps the raw postings in Parquet, split by month.

Splitting a table that way only saves work if the engine skips the folders a filter rules out, so I tested it. I wrote one month's files straight to storage, registered them with MSCK REPAIR TABLE as the 21st partition, then filtered on June 2025 and read the query plan. The plan pruned to a single partition, and the query returned only June's postings.

So the split pays off where it counts: a one-month question costs 3,015 rows of reading instead of all 60,000, and the plan itself shows it.

If you split a table by month, how do you confirm the engine actually skips the other partitions?

subject: AI Model Observability & Fairness Audits
text:
A drift alert is only worth something if you act on it. Acting on mine ended the run at 83% accuracy instead of 66%.

AI Model Observability & Fairness Audits is a portfolio project that watches a deployed classifier's inputs and decisions every day: drift tests on the features, bias checks by gender and age group, and a table of flagged problems a reviewer reads instead of every metric. I built it to learn how the whole monitoring system fits together, not just one piece, because with AI changing how work gets done, an engineer has to keep adapting.

It runs on simulated data: 60 days of predictions, with drift injected partway through. A Kolmogorov-Smirnov test raised the first alert on day 40, without waiting for any outcome labels. That left a decision to make: keep the deployed model, or retrain it.

So I replayed the rest of the run both ways. The catch is that outcomes arrive late, so the retrained version could only learn from the most recent week of labels, each one 7 days old.

Left alone, the model slid from 99.88% accuracy to 66%. Retrained every day on those delayed labels, it finished at 83%, and its total accuracy shortfall over the period was 32.6% smaller.

The alert now triggers that daily retrain, so recovery starts the day the data shifts, not when someone notices accuracy falling.

If you monitor a model whose labels arrive late, do you retrain on a fixed schedule or only when a drift alert fires?

#MachineLearning #DataEngineering
alt_text: Line chart, daily accuracy after the drift alert, days 1 to 60 of a simulated run. Both lines stay near 1.0 until drift starts on day 31; the first alert fires on day 40. Left as is, accuracy falls to 0.66 by day 60; retrained daily on week-old labels, it ends at 0.83. Simulated data.

subject: Sales Analytics & RFM Customer Segmentation Pipeline
text:
Three of four customer clusters differed mainly in recency, while only one stood far apart on frequency and spend.

Sales Analytics & RFM Customer Segmentation Pipeline is a personal portfolio project that models transaction data in a star-schema database for business intelligence reporting. Total sales tell how much a business sells, but not who buys. I built this project to learn how to find real customer groups in transaction data instead of guessing them.

Before sending segment labels downstream to reports, I needed to check if recency, frequency, and monetary value features actually split accounts into clear categories.

So I clustered scaled RFM features for 2,000 synthetic accounts using K-Means with four groups. The four clusters explained 93.9% of the variance in the scaled features, while a two-dimensional PCA view kept 99.6% of that variance. One group of 400 VIP Champions stood far apart on spend and purchase count, whereas the remaining three categories shared similar activity levels and differed mostly in recency.

Because the features separated buyers so clearly, segment names are written back to the customer dimension in the star schema for the Power BI dashboard.

Marketing teams can now use a persona slicer in the Power BI report to isolate the 400 VIP Champions for targeted retention campaigns.

When segmenting customer data for business intelligence, do you write cluster labels directly into dimension tables or generate them dynamically?

#DataEngineering #MachineLearning
alt_text: Bar chart, RFM clustering variance and cluster size: Variance explained by clusters 93.9%; Variance kept by 2‑D PCA view 99.6%.

subject: FinTech Credit Risk & Fraud Command Center
text:
Evaluating credit risk works best when high precision comes before catching every single defaulted loan.

FinTech Credit Risk & Fraud Command Center is a personal portfolio project on credit risk and fraud detection. I built it because my father took a big loss in the market when a scam that had been going on was exposed; he was collateral damage, along with many other ordinary people.

Before deploying a classifier, I needed to determine whether Random Forest or XGBoost should decline risky loan applications. Rejecting qualified applicants creates friction, so scoring every application at 0.80 or more likely to default required a clear comparison between models.

So I trained both models on the same features and scored them on a held-out 20% of the synthetic loans, logging both runs in MLflow. Random Forest reached a ROC AUC of 0.9216 compared to 0.9179 for XGBoost, while delivering 0.9341 decline precision against 0.9132. XGBoost caught more default cases with a decline recall of 0.4456 versus 0.3427, but turned away 0.1143 of all applications while Random Forest declined 0.0859.

The answer made the choice clear. Random Forest went to production because it had the higher ROC AUC and the greater precision when declining an application.

When you tune probability thresholds for risk models, do you prioritize precision to protect valid applicants or recall to catch defaults?

#MachineLearning #DataEngineering

Random Forest ROC AUC 0.9216; XGBoost ROC AUC 0.9179; Random Forest Accuracy 0.8777; XGBoost Accuracy 0.8801; Random Forest Decline precision 0.9341; XGBoost Decline precision 0.9132; Random Forest Decline recall 0.3427; XGBoost Decline recall 0.4456; Random Forest Share declined 0.0859; XGBoost Share declined 0.1143.

subject: Clinical Trials Patient Outcomes Analysis
text:
Higher dosage only matters if patients live longer. At day 365, 53.20% survived on the high dose, against 15.82% in the control group.

Clinical Trials Patient Outcomes Analysis is a personal portfolio project that runs survival statistics on 250 simulated trial patients, split into three groups: control, a low dosage and a high one. I built it because of COVID: in India's second wave, fake news and fear made things much worse, because people lacked basic clarity on how an illness works.

The first question was plain: does more of the treatment actually help? To find out, I fitted Kaplan-Meier survival curves over the full year. The catch is that many patients were still alive when the trial ended. Kaplan-Meier counts them as survivors up to day 365 instead of as deaths, and the median is read off the curve. In the high-dose group more than half were still alive, so its median is never reached.

The three separated in order. The median was 144 days for control and 288 on the lower dosage, and mortality fell in turn from 69.47% to 60.0% to 42.5%. Pairwise log-rank tests found every pair different at p < 0.05, most clearly control against the high dose (p = 1.08e-06).

That answers only half of the question, though. The same group also had the highest rate of adverse events, so the gain in survival comes with a safety cost, measured next with a chi-square test.

When a trial ends before half of a treatment's patients have died, what do you report in place of its median: survival at a fixed day, or a restricted mean?

#DataScience #MachineLearning
alt_text: Line chart, Survival by dose group: survival probability by day for each group, from the project's exports/km_curves.csv. At the end: Control 15.82%; High-dosage 53.2%; Low-dosage 33.27%. Simulated data.

subject: Automated Daily Data Insights
text:
I chose a GitHub Actions cron schedule instead of a paid server, eliminating any hosting cost.

Automated Daily Data Insights is a personal portfolio pipeline that pulls market prices each trading day, flags unusual moves with a rolling Z‑score, and publishes a report. I built it because my earlier pipelines only ran on my laptop and I wanted a job that runs by itself on real data without any server expense.

The question was whether a rolling Z‑score could reliably separate an ordinary move from a true outlier. Each daily return is compared with its 20‑day mean and flagged if it exceeds two standard deviations. On 2026‑06‑05 the return was -2.58 % with a Z‑score of 3.17, while on 2026‑05‑15 the return was -1.2 % with a score of 2.08.

Both days crossed the line, but not by the same margin: the -2.58 % day sat more than 3 standard deviations out, while the -1.2 % day only just cleared 2. When the latest trading day is an anomaly, the job automatically emails an alert with the close, the return, the score and a link to the report.

Now the pipeline runs every market day at zero hosting cost and reliably notifies me of spikes.

If you rely on free CI/CD schedules for data jobs, what strategies do you use to cope with API rate limits or occasional downtime without breaking the workflow?

#DataEngineering #MachineLearning

Two days fall outside the band and are flagged: May 15 at -1.2% (Z 2.08) and Jun 5 at -2.58% (Z 3.17). The first 20 days build the baseline and are not tested.

subject: Tax Anomaly Audit Compliance Engine
text:
A model is worth running only if it finds what a simple rule misses. Here the tax-rate rule found 45 planted errors; the model found 18.

Tax Anomaly Audit Compliance Engine is a personal portfolio project that hunts for suspicious entries in a simulated general ledger of 1,200 lines. I built it because as a new student in the US I had to file my taxes on my own, and learning how to do that is where this project came from.

It has two ways to catch a bad line. The model rates each one by how far its first digits stray from Benford's Law, the pattern real amounts tend to follow, and by how unusual an Isolation Forest finds it, then flags a risk score of 65 or more. The rule only checks whether the tax charged matches the rate for its category. So I planted anomalies and scored each layer on its own.

The rule flagged 45 lines and every one was real, catching 95.74% of the planted errors. The model flagged 19 and was right on most of them, but found only 38.3%, and the rule had already caught every one.

So the rule's flags now go first in the review order, and Benford's Law and the Isolation Forest rank the rest. A reviewer starts with flags that are certain, then works down a list sorted by risk.

When a plain business rule beats your anomaly model, do you keep the model to rank what is left or drop it?

#DataEngineering #MachineLearning

subject: Extending STEM across ASL
text:
By chance, one of 29 signs is picked right 3.45% of the time. My model got 94.83% within its top three guesses.

Extending STEM across ASL is my graduate project, peer reviewed and rebuilt on public video data, that recognises STEM and computing words in sign language. The study behind it found that only about 16% of ASL users go on to university, and missing STEM vocabulary, and too few people able to use it, was one of several main reasons.

The question was whether a model trained on a small public set could tell 29 such words apart. So I held out 2 clips of each word from 214 WLASL clips and trained on the rest. Each clip becomes MediaPipe hand landmarks plus OpenCV hand-crop features over 32 frames, read by a 1-D convolution and a bidirectional GRU.

On the held-out clips it was right 75.86% of the time on its first guess, and the correct answer was almost always among its first three guesses. Each clip took 0.34 ms of model time.

That gap decided the design. The browser page shows the top three guesses for each recording, so a wrong first guess still leaves the right answer on screen.

For gesture recognition with only a few clips per class, do you show the single top guess or several candidates?

#MachineLearning #ComputerVision
alt_text: Held-out clips named right on the first guess, by sign (2 clips each). Both right, 17 signs: computer, email, program, machine, television, write, letter, test, learn, teacher, math, calculate, measure, plus, energy, experiment, book. One of two, 10 signs: internet, print, paper, study, school, science, research, biology, physics, picture. Neither, 2 signs: network, chemistry.

history_entry.subject: Extending STEM across ASL
history_entry.text:
By chance, one of 29 signs is picked right 3.45% of the time. My model got 94.83% within its top three guesses.

Extending STEM across ASL is my graduate project, peer reviewed and rebuilt on public video data, that recognises STEM and computing words in sign language. The study behind it found that only about 16% of ASL users go on to university, and missing STEM vocabulary, and too few people able to use it, was one of several main reasons.

The question was whether a model trained on a small public set could tell 29 such words apart. So I held out 2 clips of each word from 214 WLASL clips and trained on the rest. Each clip becomes MediaPipe hand landmarks plus OpenCV hand-crop features over 32 frames, read by a 1-D convolution and a bidirectional GRU.

On the held-out clips it was right 75.86% of the time on its first guess, and the correct answer was almost always among its first three guesses. Each clip took 0.34 ms of model time.

That gap decided the design. The browser page shows the top three guesses for each recording, so a wrong first guess still leaves the right answer on screen.

For gesture recognition with only a few clips per class, do you show the single top guess or several candidates?

#MachineLearning #ComputerVision

subject: FinTech Credit Risk & Fraud Command Center
text:
An alert is only useful if you can act on it. My velocity rule was right on all 1,110 of its alerts; the amount-spike rule on 40 of 4,069.

FinTech Credit Risk & Fraud Command Center is a personal portfolio project on credit risk and fraud detection, run on simulated card transactions. I built it because my father took a big loss in the market when a scam that had been going on was exposed; he was collateral damage, along with many other ordinary people.

Before letting any check act on its own, I needed to know which ones could be trusted. Three checks read only the amount, hour, location and customer: velocity (5 or more charges inside 10 minutes), a spike over 7 times the customer's median, and a foreign location. I scored their alerts against the cases the simulator planted, which the checks never see.

Velocity never raised a false alarm but caught only 42.84% of the planted cases. Foreign location caught more, 56.5%, yet fewer than a third of its alerts were fraud. Spikes were almost all legitimate large purchases, at 0.98% precision.

So velocity is the rule trusted on its own, spikes stay a review signal rather than a block, and together the three catch every planted fraud case.

How do you decide when a fraud rule is precise enough to block a payment instead of queueing it for review?

subject: AI Model Observability & Fairness Audits
text:
Nobody reads 300 metric values a day for long. Over a 60-day run, my monitor asked a reviewer to read 25 alerts instead.

AI Model Observability & Fairness Audits is a personal portfolio project that watches a deployed classifier on simulated inference records: drift tests on its inputs and bias checks on its decisions. I built it to learn how the whole monitoring system fits together, not just one piece, because with AI changing how work gets done, I believe an engineer has to keep adapting.

The risk with monitoring is that it buries people. So each daily audit writes a row to an audit_alerts table only when a rule crosses its threshold: a KS p-value under 0.01, PSI above 0.25, disparate impact outside 0.8 to 1.25, or a true-positive-rate gap of more than 10 points between groups.

I then counted what a reviewer would read with that table against reading every daily metric. Only about a third of the days raised anything at all. The KS test fired on every one of them; PSI flagged a major shift on just 4, and later, so KS was the earlier signal on this drift.

The reviewer now works from audit_alerts alone and opens a day only when it has a row there.

If you monitor models for drift and bias, do you alert on every threshold breach or group them into a daily digest?

#MachineLearning #DataEngineering

subject: Clinical Trials Patient Outcomes Analysis
text:
The dose that kept the most patients alive also hurt the most. Adverse events hit 23.75% on the high dose, against 8.42% on control.

Clinical Trials Patient Outcomes Analysis is a personal portfolio project that runs survival and safety statistics on simulated trial patients in three groups: control, a low dosage and a high one. I built it because of COVID: in India's second wave, fake news and fear made things much worse, because people lacked basic clarity on how an illness works.

The survival test had already shown the high dose living longest. That answer felt incomplete, though: a treatment is only better if its benefit outweighs its harm, so I needed to know whether side effects rose with the dosage.

So I counted adverse events in each group and ran a chi-square test of independence on them. The low dosage sat close to control at 10.67%, while the highest one more than doubled it. The test put the chance of a gap this large arising by luck at p = 0.008807.

The result changed how the report reads. The longer survival now sits beside its safety cost, so whoever reads it weighs the two together instead of seeing one side alone.

When a treatment improves one outcome but worsens another, how do you present the trade-off to people who are not statisticians?

#DataScience #Healthcare

subject: TalentVenue EventIntel
text:
An 86.20% accurate model can still miss half of what matters. Mine flagged contract cancellations with a recall of only 0.48.

TalentVenue EventIntel is my capstone for the ElevateMe Bootcamp data analytics certificate, built on a real event and talent-management company's database. It came with real problems: reports recalculated money totals one booking at a time on every read, payments could not easily be checked against the ledger, and 14.7% of deals were cancelled.

That last number was the one I wanted to predict. So I engineered features from the staged tables, split them 80/20 with stratification, and trained a Random Forest of 100 trees. Of the 2,000 held-out records, 352 were cancelled.

The headline accuracy looked strong, and the ROC-AUC of 0.8707 says the model ranks risk well. But most bookings complete, so accuracy flatters it: at the default threshold it caught about half of the cancellations, and 0.65 of its cancellation flags were right.

So it runs as a Snowflake Python UDF, scoring each one inside SQL where analysts already work, and a TypeScript CLI checks the feature-mappings file before the dashboard reads it. The score sorts the pipeline by risk rather than deciding on its own.

When most of your outcomes are the common class, which metric do you put in front of the business first?

subject: Member Messages QA System
text:
My Q&A system told me Hans needed 20 front-row seats. The number came from a date, November 20.

The Member Messages QA System was my first chatbot-style project, and a basic one on purpose. Answers about people are usually buried in loose messages: a booking here, a phone number there. I wanted to see whether a small system could find the person first and then the message that holds it, without a language model making up the answer.

So it pairs semantic search with spaCy name matching, and I checked it on 26 hand-written questions. The first run got 22 right, 85%. Reading the misses, the extraction rules treated dates as quantities and did not know number words like "four". Hans got the seat answer above, and two related questions about him were wrong too.

I changed the rules to skip dates and accept number words, then ran the same questions again: 25 right, 96%.

The evaluation now runs in CI, so if a later rule change brings the date problem back, the build fails before anyone reads a wrong count.

When you test extraction rules, do you write the tricky questions yourself or collect them from real users?

#NLP #DataEngineering

subject: Real-Time IoT Telematics Predictive Maintenance
text:
An alarm on every odd reading gets ignored. A rolling z-score caught 210 of 214 planted spikes with few false flags.

Real-Time IoT Telematics Predictive Maintenance is a personal portfolio project that monitors simulated vehicle telemetry from 5 devices. A sensor that drifts or jumps can mean a failing part, and I wanted to learn whether a simple rolling z-score could catch real spikes without flooding a fleet with false alarms. It was also my first time handling data that never stops arriving, in micro-batches.

So I flagged any battery-temperature or motor-vibration value whose z-score, over the last 50 readings, passed 3, and matched the flags against spikes the simulator planted and the detector never sees. Across 11,315 readings it raised 232 flags.

Precision came out at 90.52% and recall at 98.13%. The detector did slightly better on vibration, 99.06%, than on temperature, 97.22%, which was close enough to keep one method for both.

So the same threshold of 3 now runs on both sensors, and a warning repeats at most every 4 hours while a condition lasts, which gave 404 maintenance alerts across the fleet for the month.

For streaming telemetry, do you tune one anomaly threshold per sensor type or keep a single shared one?

subject: Multi-State Land Use Emissions Analysis
text:
Vectorising my shock detector cut its time by 51.65%. On a much larger set, the saving fell to 24.24%.

Multi-State Land Use Emissions Analysis started because land use, like forests burning or land turning into suburbs, changes how much carbon a state stores or releases, and I wanted to learn how that is measured from public data. The pipeline runs on the EPA's state inventory for 5 states.

One step flags shock days: a value that jumps away from its rolling median. I first wrote it as a Python function called once per series, then as grouped pandas operations. For timing I used simulated series shaped like the real data, at the project's own scale and at 50 states over 3 years.

At 5,350 records the grouped version took 9.5 ms against 19.6 ms. At 273,750 records it took 307.6 ms against 406.1 ms. Faster both times, but the gap narrowed as the data grew, so I would not promise the same saving at any scale.

Speed alone was not enough to switch. A test checks that both versions flag exactly the same days, and they do. With that in place, the grouped pandas code is what the pipeline uses.

When you replace a loop with a vectorised version, what do you check besides the timing?

subject: AI-ML Data Science Simulation
text:
A store that reorders from last week's sales runs out when demand moves. A forecast cut stock-out days from 51 to 20 in my test.

AI-ML Data Science Simulation is a personal portfolio project that forecasts daily demand for 5 branches on simulated sales data. I wanted to learn whether a prediction actually beats that habit, and by how much, before trusting one.

Accuracy on a chart was not enough; what matters to a store is shelves. So I replayed reordering on the held-out period both ways: every Monday, shelves were topped up to last week's sales plus 10%, or to the Random Forest forecast plus 10%, and each day's sales were drawn from what was there.

The habit filled 92.1% of orders; the forecast filled 99.5%, with far fewer units short and less left unsold each week. Almost all the gain came in promotion weeks, which last week's sales cannot see coming but the published calendar can.

So the model's prediction drives the reorder, with the promotion calendar as one of its inputs, and fewer shelves run empty while less sits unsold.

When you replace a rule of thumb with a forecast for reordering, do you judge it on stock-outs, on leftover stock, or both?

subject: Tax Anomaly Audit Compliance Engine
text:
Same checks, same answers, very different wait. On 100,000 ledger entries, column operations beat a row-by-row loop by 99.86%.

Tax Anomaly Audit Compliance Engine is a personal portfolio project that checks a simulated general ledger for bad entries before anything else reads it. I built it because as a new student in the US I had to file my taxes on my own, and learning how to do that is where this project came from.

The rules are plain: required fields present, a positive value, a date inside the ledger year, an account that belongs to its department, no duplicates, and tax equal to the category rate times the amount. The question was how to run them, one row at a time in a loop, or as operations over whole columns.

So I ran the same rules both ways. The column version won by a wide margin, and the result was the part that mattered: both flagged exactly the same 3,405 invalid entries, so the speed cost nothing in accuracy.

So the pipeline's validation step runs as column operations, and a full ledger pass now fits inside every run instead of being saved for occasional batches.

When you rewrite a slow row-by-row check, how do you prove the faster version flags exactly the same records?

subject: Sentence Transformers
text:
Fine-tuning does not change everything a model says. My LoRA adapter changed 1 of 5 held-out answers and left 4 of 5 identical.

This is a personal portfolio project where I built a sentence transformer myself on Small BERT, because using ready-made embedding models left me not knowing what happens inside them. Then I wanted to know what fine-tuning really changes, so I trained a LoRA adapter on Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on a free Colab T4 GPU.

It was small: rank 16, on the attention projections only, trained on 540 examples from Databricks Dolly-15k with 60 held out. Training loss fell from 1.779 to 1.650 over three epochs, which says it learned something, but not what.

Next I asked the base version and the tuned one the same held-out instructions with greedy decoding, so any difference would come from the fine-tuning alone. The one answer that changed was open-ended: fun things to do in New York City. The short factual prompts came back exactly as before.

So I report it as it is: a small adapter on 540 examples changes how it answers open questions, not what it knows. A test now checks that at least one prompt changes, so a broken run is caught.

When you fine-tune a small model, how do you check what actually changed beyond the training loss?

subject: FinTech Credit Risk & Fraud Command Center
text:
A risk score that arrives after the applicant clicks submit protects no one. Mine comes back in 67 ms at the median.

The FinTech Credit Risk & Fraud Command Center is personal for me. My father took a big loss in the market when a scam that had been going on was exposed; he was collateral damage, along with many other ordinary people. Catching risk only helps if the check runs while the decision is still open.

So the question I tested was whether the scoring API is fast enough to sit inside an application flow. I called POST /api/predict 200 times on a laptop. With the model loaded once at startup and cached, the median was 67 ms and the 95th percentile was 85 ms.

The other option was loading the model on every request. I chose to load it once at startup and keep it in memory, so each call only pays for the scoring itself.

A fast number on one day is not a promise, though. The build limit is 100 ms for the median, and a test fails CI if latency reaches it, so a slower change cannot slip in unnoticed.

Where do you set the latency limit for a model inside a live flow, and who decides it?

subject: Automated Daily Data Insights
text:
A free scheduler is only useful if it keeps running. Mine has run 124 times since June, and all 124 succeeded.

Automated Daily Data Insights is a personal portfolio project that runs by itself every trading day: it pulls market prices, flags unusual days and commits a chart and a report. Most pipelines I had built ran once on my laptop, so I wanted one that runs on real data with no server to pay for, and to see whether a free GitHub Actions schedule is reliable enough for that.

Hosted runners fail in ordinary ways: a network blip, a rate limit, a day with no new close. So the script fetches 60 days of prices with up to three retries, skips a day that brings nothing new, and drops any row with a missing value before it reaches the report. Each of those has its own test.

The record from 2026-06-19 to 2026-10-20 is the answer. Every scheduled run finished, and none produced a wrong report.

subject: Extending STEM across ASL
text:
My sign recognition model takes 8.9 ms. The whole request takes 1090.5 ms, and almost none of that wait is the model.

Extending STEM across ASL comes from a study behind the project: only about 16% of ASL users go on to higher education at a university, and a lack of signs for STEM terms, and of people who know them, was one of several main reasons. This project recognises word signs from webcam video.

For it to work live, the answer has to come back while the person is still signing. So I sent 20 requests of 30 JPEG frames each, a two-second recording, to the /recognize-sign endpoint and timed every stage on a laptop CPU.

Decoding the frames took 76.2 ms at the median. Extracting hand features took 997.0 ms. The model itself was the smallest stage of all.

The hand landmarker is where the time goes, so that is what I changed: it is built once and reused across requests. Every answer also returns its time per stage, so the next slow step shows up in the response itself.

When the slowest step in a pipeline is the preprocessing rather than the model, where do you look first to speed it up?

#ComputerVision #Accessibility
